title: Corey Ruiz's family should guide police legislation, Stubbs says - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. More than a month after Madison police shot and killed 38-year-old Corey Ruiz, Democratic state Rep. Shelia Stubbs said she is following his family’s lead on any legislative actions she could take in the next session in response to the shooting. Ruiz, a Black man from Madison, was shot and killed by Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson on July 22 at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets. Officers chased Ruiz, who was on a bicycle, after being called to the neighborhood for a person who was checking parked cars. They eventually intercepted Ruiz at the east side intersection where a physical struggle took place in the street. Officials say Ruiz pulled out a knife and injured Baitinger-Peterson, who then shot Ruiz after two other officers deployed a Taser “without success.” Stubbs quickly stood by Ruiz’s family’s side in support and was among the first lawmakers to speak out on the incident. She represents parts of Madison, Monona and McFarland in the state Assembly. She has served in the Assembly since 2019 and is up for reelection in November, running against Republican Henry Johnson, a student at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. During her time as a lawmaker, Stubbs has been a leading advocate for racial equity and police reform, and she’s been in office during several incidents of violent police encounters with Black men, including the 2015 shooting death of Tony Robinson Jr. in Madison, the 2020 death of George Floyd in Minneapolis and the 2020 shooting of Jacob Blake in Kenosha. Everett Mitchell, a Dane County Circuit Court judge and senior pastor of Christ the Solid Rock Church, adds votives to the base of the Vel Phillips statue during a demostration for Corey Ruiz, held by the African American Council of Churches at the Wisconsin Capitol. If she is reelected to a fifth term, Stubbs said she has ideas on legislation she could propose next session stemming from Ruiz’s death, such as changes to state laws relating to body-worn cameras, mental health, fleeing and eluding, and oversight committees. She also criticized the city of Madison for not having body cameras and not participating in a 2022 grant program to help police departments buy the video equipment. But ultimately, she said, it is up to Ruiz’s family members and their attorney, well-known civil rights lawyer Ben Crump, to shape any specific changes they want in state law. “It’s whatever they want,” Stubbs told the Cap Times. “I will be introducing whatever it is that they ask of me.” In 2020, Republican Assembly Speaker Robin Vos appointed Stubbs to co-chair a legislative task force on racial disparities, which Vos created in response to the global outrage that followed Floyd’s death. The task force introduced a package of 18 bills that included reforms such as requiring crisis intervention training and drug testing of police officers. Nine of the task force’s bills were enacted into law, including a new statewide standard for law enforcement use of force, a restriction on choke holds and new requirements for police agencies to track data on incidents such as use of force and no-knock search warrants. Rep. Shelia Stubbs previously co-chaired a legislative task force on racial disparities following the 2020 death of George Floyd. “It was a start,” Stubbs said of the task force’s accomplishments. “By all means it wasn’t meant to be the final bills. I think you learn from every incident.” In addition to Stubbs and other legislators, the 32-person task force included pastors, police, protesters, nonprofit leaders, educators and a diverse group of community members. It was important to bring many different voices and stakeholders to the table, Stubbs said. Stubbs said others told her it was “political suicide” to serve on the task force, but she felt it was important for her to be part of the conversation because of her own experiences as a Black woman. “What I did know is I believed in change, and what I did know is I couldn’t sit around and just not do something, right? And that’s where I’m at with the Ruiz family. I want to do what it takes for outcomes. We couldn’t save Corey,” Stubbs said. “But we can save the next person, because we have an opportunity. And I think what people have to do is take accountability.” One of the task force bills from 2021 that did become law established a one-year grant program for Wisconsin police agencies to buy body-worn cameras. In total, 48 agencies across the state were awarded grants from the program in 2023, totaling more than $1.2 million, according to data provided by the Wisconsin Department of Justice. Some Madison-area agencies applied for and received a grant, including the city of Middleton, the village of Belleville and Iowa County. The Madison Police Department, the only law enforcement agency in Dane County that does not widely use body cameras, did not apply for this state grant. Stubbs called it “unacceptable” that the city’s police officers did not have body-worn cameras at the time of Ruiz’s death. “We created the state funding opportunity,” Stubbs said of the grant program. “Madison Police Department has to own up to it that they didn’t seize the opportunity.” She added: “When people say, ‘What is the state doing?’ We did something. What did the municipality do? They failed to apply.” City officials have debated the body cameras' use for years, with worries over costs and potential misuse of footage. In 2024, the city participated in a pilot program, equipping 41 police officers with body cameras for 90 days. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said she plans to include funding for body-worn cameras in the next budget, and the city plans to apply for a federal grant to help with the purchase of the equipment. But long-term costs to operate a body-worn camera program present a challenge for the city, the mayor said, and state revenue restrictions on municipalities add to that hurdle. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway speaks at a press conference after an encampment at the memorial for Corey Ruiz was cleared by the city. “Trained staff will be needed to manage and maintain the equipment, as well as preserve, catalog and store the video footage so it’s available to the public. Those costs must come out of the city’s operating budget. Local governments in Wisconsin are severely restricted financially by the state. Rising costs make it a challenge just to continue the services we are already providing to Madison residents,” Rhodes-Conway said. “The lack of options provided by the state makes adding anything new to our operating budget — particularly staff — very difficult.” Stubbs said the state’s grant program was successful and that she is willing to look at other legislation around body cameras such as another grant or a requirement that local governments buy and use them. But again, she said, she wants Ruiz’s family to decide. Ruiz’s death opened old wounds for Stubbs, who said the shooting harkened back to other trauma her community has felt, like the deaths of Robinson and Floyd, and the Abundant Life Christian School shooting in 2024, which happened in her district. Stubbs recalled protesting and marching late into the evening after Floyd’s death. “During that time it was just really traumatic. It was draining. It was emotional,” Stubbs said. “I’m not afraid to share I cried a lot.” But she said she is taking lessons from the past as the community navigates what’s next after Ruiz’s death. She learned through those experiences and on the task force that leaders need to listen to the community. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. “That’s what I think people look for at a moment like this, that you at least show up. When you are elected, you got to show up to work,” she said. “You gotta face the heat.” She said she also remains focused on writing policy that will become law. For years, Republicans have controlled the state Legislature and the proposals that move in and out of both chambers. But Democrats have had their eyes set on winning a trifecta this fall — controlling the Assembly, the Senate and the governorship — which Stubbs said will “absolutely” make it easier for reforms to be implemented. “I look forward to being in the majority, and I look forward to getting work done across this state that has just been on a hiatus,” Stubbs said.

title: Gregory McClain Appointed Civil Rights Director - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release September 3, 2026  Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway is appointing Gregory McClain to be the Director of the Department of Civil Rights. McClain is an Air Force veteran and most recently served as the Equal Opportunity Manager for Montgomery County Government in Rockville, Maryland.   “Greg will be a fantastic addition to the Department of Civil Rights. His journey to civil rights work makes him well-qualified to lead this agency with a data-driven approach focused on results for our residents," said Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway.   McClain has more than a decade of experience in advancing racial equity, social justice, equal employment, and public health initiatives. He has a Bachelor of Science in biomedical sciences and master's degrees in business and health Administration from Oklahoma State University. Additionally, while earning a master's degree in public health at UW-Madison, McClain worked in the community to prevent harm to veterans and others suffering from substance use disorders, as well as to advance health equity.   “I'm grateful for the opportunity to serve Madison residents and grow the impact of the Department of Civil Rights. Starting from a place of honesty and transparency, I see my role as ensuring it's a great city for everyone," said McClain. “I fully intend to be a champion of the department and can't wait to amplify the important work being done by its dedicated staff."   McClain is also excited for the community to meet his service dog, Flash. He was matched with the three-year-old Bernese Mountain Dog as part of the K9s for Warriors program.   The appointment is contingent on McClain's contract being approved by the Madison Common Council. title: State Rep Shelia Stubbs calls for mandatory body-worn cameras for all Wisconsin police - Madison365
text: State Representative Shelia Stubbs said this morning that she will champion legislation to require body-worn cameras for all police in Wisconsin. At a press conference at the Center for Black Excellence and Culture Thursday morning, Stubbs, who represents Madison’s South Side in the State Assembly, said the City of Madison has “failed” by not implementing body-worn cameras, and by not even applying for state funding to implement them. But, she said, any legislation to increase or require implementation would be guided by the wishes of the family of Corey Ruiz, the man killed by Madison police on July 22. “Any legislation that we put forth for Corey’s legacy will be done with the blessings of his family and their advocates,” Stubbs said. “It is unacceptable that in 2026, Madison Police Department still does not have body cameras for all of its officers. That’s the bottom line,” she said. “You can’t just tell me your priorities. You need to demonstrate your priorities with action and with investment.” Stubbs appeared alongside Ruiz’s mother and sister, their attorneys Ben Crump and B’Ivory Lamarr, and Madison Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass. All said that implementation of body-worn cameras must be accompanied by strong policy that will actually enable transparency and accountability. “Transparency plus accountability equals trust, and that is what was put on full display in the aftermath of the killing of Corey Ruiz was the apparent lack of trust between the community and the police,” Crump said. Policies that allow for accountability exist elsewhere, Crump said. “This is not a situation where we have to go and reinvent the wheel,” Lamarr said, noting that the City of Milwaukee police department policy requires body-worn camera video from critical incidents be shared with the victim’s family within 48 hours and released publicly within 15 days. Citing state law, City of Madison Attorney Michael Haas has said no evidence from critical incidents can be released to anyone, including Glass’s office, until after the state Division of Criminal Justice has completed its investigation of the incident. “I want body-worn cameras as much as anyone else,” Glass said. “It will make my job a lot easier because right now I have to listen to the lies that come across my desk every single day because it’s not in a video.”  She noted that Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway’s executive budget proposal for 2027 includes funding to implement body-worn cameras, but that the policy discussion hasn’t happened yet. “The budget for body worn cameras is in the mayor’s upcoming budget. … They’re trying to put it under the radar so that the policy is not there,” she said. Stubbs said she won’t formally introduce legislation until the new Assembly term convenes in January. She said she intends to work with a bipartisan group of legislators to implement body-worn cameras statewide. “It is unacceptable in 2026 [that] our community continues to be traumatized and retraumatized by the city’s failure to take meaningful action,” she said.

title: West Mifflin apartment building opens with tribute to historic house it replaced - Wisconsin State Journal
text: A nonprofit Madison housing developer this week celebrated the opening of a Downtown apartment building aimed at middle-income workers, featuring an imaginative tribute to a historic house the building replaced. Of the 40 units at Madison Development Corporation’s four-story, $11.2 million Bankston Apartments, 30 are reserved for households making no more than 80% of Dane County’s area median income, or no more than about $75,800 for a one-person household or $108,200 for a four-person household. The building, at 429 W. Mifflin St., is named after longtime MDC board member Vicki Bankston. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, who spoke at a ribbon-cutting for the Bankston on Thursday, noted that the building was fully leased two months before it opened. “Keep going,” she said. “We need more of this.” The redevelopment project sparked a campaign by local scientist Peter Taglia and his neighbors to relocate a nearly century-old brick house designed by a noted Madison architect from its original location at 427 W. Mifflin St. Ultimately, Taglia ran out of time to move the house, and it was demolished last summer. Taglia attended the ribbon-cutting for the Bankston. He said it took him some time to move past the loss of the house. “It’s bittersweet,” he said. “But what a cool thing they did there.” Developers used a photograph of the house and its real, refurbished front door to re-create part of the facade inside the Bankston’s fourth-floor community room, which is dedicated to historian Stu Levitan, another longtime board member. On display in the building’s entryway are a stained-glass window from another, less historic house that was also demolished to make way for the project and photographs of memorable moments on West Mifflin Street. Peter Taglia was unable to relocate this 1920s-era West Mifflin Street home before it was demolished to make way for a lower-cost apartment building. text: A tenth Madison Fire Department ambulance is now in service, stationed in downtown Madison. Medic 1, located at Fire Station 1 (316 West Dayton Street), will serve the busy downtown district while also addressing the increasing demand for emergency medical services across the city. The overarching goal with the addition of the tenth medic unit was to identify the location where it may have the biggest positive impact across the entire system. Our data analysis left no doubt that Fire Station 1 was the optimal place to assign our tenth ambulance. Chris Carbon, Fire Chief, Madison Fire Department In 2025, Fire Station 1's response area generated 3,770 emergency medical calls. However, each of these calls was handled by ambulances from other fire stations.  The existing demand for emergency medical service in this area, combined with analysis showing the positive benefit across the city, made Fire Station 1 the best possible location for service expansion. The addition of a tenth ambulance strengthens our support of safety, health, and well-being, particularly in the downtown area. I'm thrilled to welcome this new ambulance to Fire Station 1. Satya Rhodes-Conway, Madison Mayor With the placement of Medic 1 downtown, projected call volumes and drive times of all medic units in the city are expected to decrease. Overall total call volume continues to increase for the Madison Fire Department.  The department will continue to monitor call volume and the utilization of all ten ambulances to ensure that emergency medical resources are being deployed most appropriately across the city. As our vibrant downtown continues to grow, so does the need for quick fire and EMS response when emergencies happen. The return of Medic 1 to Fire Station 1 is a very welcome addition to the area, and I'm comforted to know that overall service capacity will improve across the city with Medic 1 in place. title: Family of Corey Ruiz continues to demand accountability from Madison leaders - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. — The family of Corey Ruiz is calling for the Madison Police Department to implement body-worn cameras after the 38-year-old was shot and killed by a Madison police officer on July 22. Ruiz’s mother and sister joined civil rights attorney Ben Crump on Thursday morning to again demand justice for Ruiz. They said their lack of trust in Madison police stems from what they view as a lack of accountability. Crump said Ruiz’s death exposed what he called “the apparent lack of trust between the community and the police.” “In 2026, in Madison, Wisconsin, the police don’t have body camera videos,” Crump said. No body camera footage of the shooting is available because the Madison Police Department does not require officers to wear body-worn cameras. State Rep. Shelia Stubbs, D-Madison, said city leaders have failed to invest in the technology. “When given the opportunity, time and time again the City of Madison has failed to make the investments necessary to equip officers with critical technology,” Stubbs said. Stubbs said that if officers had been wearing body cameras on July 22, the community would have a clearer picture of what happened. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway has said she intends to include funding for a body-worn camera program in the 2027 city budget. She said Madison police plan to apply for a federal grant program, and those funds would help purchase the equipment. “Trained staff will be needed to manage and maintain the equipment, as well as preserve, catalog and store the video footage so it’s available to the public. Those costs must come out of the City’s operating budget. Local governments in Wisconsin are severely restricted financially by the State. Rising costs make it a challenge just to continue the services we are already providing to Madison residents. The lack of options provided by the State makes adding anything new to our operating budget — particularly staff — very difficult,” Rhodes-Conway said in a statement. Interim Independent Police Monitor Aeiramique Glass said she supports body cameras but said the city also needs a strong policy guiding how they are used. “We have to demand that there is a strong, comprehensive policy that the community is a part of and engaged in, and leading on how these tools will be utilized in this city,” Glass said. Crump said the Ruiz family wants any body camera policy to include a requirement for when video must be released. “We want to make sure that there’s a policy that will mandate when the body cam video will be released,” Crump said. The investigation into Ruiz’s death remains ongoing. The last public update came Aug. 10, when the Department of Justice said the Division of Criminal Investigation was continuing to review evidence and determine the facts of the incident. When the investigation is complete, all materials will be turned over to the Dane County District Attorney’s Office for a decision on any potential charges.

text: City of Madison Home Departments All Departments Assessor's Office Attorney's Office Building Inspection CDA Housing Civil Rights Clerk's Office Common Council Community Development Economic Development Employee Assistance Program Engineering Finance Fire Fleet Golf Goodman Pool Human Resources Independent Police Monitor Information Technology Madison City Channel Madison Public Library Madison Senior Center Mayor's Office Metro Transit Monona Terrace Community & Convention Center Municipal Court Olbrich Botanical Gardens Parking Parks Planning & Community & Economic Development Planning Police Public Health Madison & Dane County Public Works Streets & Urban Forestry Traffic Engineering Transportation Treasury Warner Park Community Recreation Center Water Utility Report a Problem Services Jobs Accounts Contact Search Leave this field blank Menu City of Madison City of Madison News Live & Work Health & Safety Visit & Play Business & Development Get Around City Hall Projects Vision City of Madison / News / Mayor Rhodes-Conway Releases 2027 Executive Capital Budget Mayor Rhodes-Conway Releases 2027 Executive Capital Budget posted  September 8, 2026 – 3:28pm For Immediate Release September 8, 2026 "The City of Madison's 2027 Capital Budget and five-year Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) outline infrastructure investments that uplift our entire community and are essential for a thriving city. The funding in this proposal provides residents with housing and transportation options so they can decide what works best for their families. It underpins our local economy and attracts innovative employers and businesses. It also furthers our goals to build a more resilient city. And by investing wisely in our facilities, it allows city staff to more efficiently provide critical services that we all depend on. My 2027 Executive Capital Budget proposal reflects years of strategic planning that is firmly grounded in the values and aspirations of the people of Madison. It's my honor to present it to the community and their elected representatives on the Madison Common Council for approval.   The public will have multiple opportunities to weigh in on the Executive Capital Budget, as well as my 2027 Executive Operating Budget, which focuses on services, staffing, and programs and will be introduced in October. Both budgets will have public hearings and be considered by Alders, first at the Finance Committee and then before the full Council.   The City of Madison continues to be fiscally healthy thanks to our commitment to supporting essential services and infrastructure improvements, conservative financial management, and a strong regional economy that benefits the entire state. This is reflected in the City's Triple-A bond rating from Moody's, which ensures we have the lowest possible borrowing costs and results in millions in savings over the life of a bond. It's a delicate balancing act to prepare for the needs of a growing city while keeping our debt payments, felt in the operating budget, at a sustainable level.   Due to cutbacks in funding from state and federal governments, the burden of maintaining critical infrastructure is falling too heavily on local property taxpayers. When coupled with high inflation, local governments simply cannot keep up. Just as our residents are experiencing, the high costs of construction materials are also hitting the City's bottom line. We need bipartisan policies that invest in the American people and the places they call home, rather than starting wars and tariff fights abroad. There is nothing controversial or political about effective stormwater infrastructure, roads free of potholes, or adequate facilities to provide emergency services. In fact, deferring these investments comes with real costs to our quality of life, our economy, and our health.   With this in mind, my Executive Budget is $90.6 million lower in general obligation borrowing, supported by the general fund, than what was originally requested by city agencies. To be clear, the original agency requests are for projects that are long overdue and would benefit the entire city. My administration will continue to seek out both opportunities for increased efficiency and every available opportunity for outside investments in infrastructure. I'm proud that since I was first elected, we have secured more than $750 million in federal and state funding, which has helped fund critical infrastructure while lessening the impact on local taxpayers. I'm hopeful that these opportunities will become more frequent in the future, and City staff are doing the planning work so we are ready to capture these funds if and when they become available. Because when Madison is successful, that success is shared far beyond our city limits.  In the meantime, the goals of our five-year capital improvement plan are focused on creating more homes, saving future operating budget dollars by modernizing a few key facilities, and investing in public safety.   Like many growing cities across the country, Madison needs to diversify the type of homes available to existing and future residents. We will continue to confront this challenge head-on and use all tools at our disposal. One way we are doing so is by creating more housing. The Triangle Redevelopment will nearly quadruple the number of homes for working families at that location and, because of sustainability features, renters will see long-term savings on their utility bills. This ambitious, generational investment in social housing is in addition to the $87.8 million we are including in the affordable housing fund and will help meet our goal of creating 15,000 more homes by 2030. We are doing everything we can as a local government to bend the curve on the rising costs for renters and first-time homeowners. Despite our efforts, the consequences of federal government disinvestment are felt acutely by cities like Madison. Like many in our community, I'm deeply frustrated by the affordability crisis and the associated costs of mitigating the problem instead of solving it. We need support at the state and federal level to reach long-term stability in the housing market and I'm eager to work in partnership with these entities to make it happen.  The upgraded Streets facility on South Point Road on the far west side is an excellent example of how capital spending can save taxpayers millions in future operating budgets. This facility will cut hundreds of hours per year in the travel time and associated fuel costs it takes for both trash and recycling pickup, as well as snow and ice removal for a large portion of the city. In this capital budget, there is a modest amount for remodeling the Streets Division's Badger Road facility to complete the final transition steps of the South Point Road project and create a permanent home for Parking Enforcement. We are also taking preliminary steps toward finding a long-term solution to updating the outdated Traffic Engineering facility on Sayle Street. Evaluating the long-term needs of our city and potential operations savings will be at the forefront of this process. Additionally, the City's ambitious Park & Badger redevelopment remains on track. This project is slated to replace the outdated Fire Station 6 with a modern facility, create a new public health clinic, and fund hundreds more affordable homes. It has already created space for Madison College to build a new childcare training facility that will increase the number of providers in our area.   Also included in my Executive Budget is funding to launch a body-worn camera program for the Madison Police Department. Chief John Patterson has indicated this is his number one priority for his department. Throughout this year, many alders have also communicated their support for body-worn cameras. Even before the recent death of a community member at the hands of the police brought this issue to the forefront of public attention, this item was included in my Executive Budget because of the clear support from the Council and Chief Patterson's efforts to lessen the significant operating budget impact needed to implement this program. Body-worn cameras are not the only police accountability measure that Madison needs to consider in the weeks and months ahead. However, I think it's time to take a step forward on this long-debated equipment decision, which is why I included funding for this technology in this year's capital budget.   The 2027 Executive Capital Budget prioritizes projects in the following areas:   I want to thank city staff for their thoughtful and creative work during this year's Capital budget process. I'm looking forward to the process of briefing the community and the Common Council on this budget, and to seeing what amendments my Council colleagues have before it is finalized in November. " — Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway Subscribe to the City of Madison News Releases email list. title: Here's where Madison residents could feel city budget pinch - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. A review of city budget proposals paints a stark portrait of Madison that could include a hiring freeze, Sundays with no library access, reduced bilingual support and fewer public safety officers in 2027. Other cuts could curtail initiatives like the Transportation Department’s “Ride the Drive” event, as well as reduce City Council members’ pay, trash collection in the parks and air quality monitoring. Madison’s city leaders anticipate making significant changes to next year’s capital budget that funds major projects, as well as the operating budget that pays for daily programs, services and personnel costs. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway released her Executive Capital Budget this week and is expected to share her proposed operating budget in October. The city’s annual operating budget for 2027 is projected at around $483 million — about $11 million more than expected revenue. Rhodes-Conway urged department heads to cut costs by at least 2% for next year while aligning with the city’s data-informed strategic framework, called Results Madison. Agency leaders also are expected to help the city ensure efficiencies and comply with strict state spending limits. As part of Results Madison this year, six agencies are undergoing a review of their internal structures and deliverables to taxpayers, including the Office of the Independent Monitor, the City Attorney’s Office and the Parking and Water Utility departments. Some agencies will likely face administrative cutbacks and reduced capacity to fund interns or attend conventions, while others might have to seek funding elsewhere for initiatives, according to city budget documents. What should Madison prioritize in its 2027 budget? Share your thoughts via email to: enururdin@captimes.com City agency leaders submitted their projections in July for the cost to continue programs and services next year. While operating budget hearings aren’t until November, there’s already been some buzz urging city leaders to take a more equitable and community-centered approach to the budget rather than make standardized reductions. A Cap Times review of the operating budget requests identified several potential cuts to services and programs that would affect residents and city workers. Read the city’s budget book here The majority of the city’s budget goes to public safety and the personnel who respond to emergencies and work in the Fire, Police and Public Health departments. Public Health Madison & Dane County plans to eliminate solely county-funded Narcan — the anti-overdose drug — and leave several positions vacant. Fire Department Chief Chris Carbon said he struggled to find cuts in the agency largely because of increased need for emergency response and specific requirements the department has to meet to receive state funding that measure response times, staffing, training and budget efficiencies. The department is anticipating rollout of the city’s 10th ambulance later this year, and budget cuts could mean having to postpone it and eliminating a CARES team — both of which are needed to respond to increasing calls to service. CARES is the Community Alternative Response Emergency program that sends behavioral health specialists to crisis situations. The Public Safety Review Committee has struggled to reach a meeting quorum amid concerns over the Corey Ruiz shooting and city budget cuts. Cuts to the Police Department’s $104 million budget could diminish the Traffic Enforcement and Safety Team, or members from the violent crime investigation or the community outreach teams. Police Chief John Patterson said in his memo that he hopes to continue a pilot program that so far has created six part-time positions for officers wanting flexible options. Five of the six have been filled, and he hopes the department can continue offering diverse options to meet the needs of the community and workforce. The police chief is requesting funding for body-worn cameras in the capital budget this year. Patterson estimates the cost to implement the cameras over three years will amount to about $415,000, not including five additional full-time staff and $100,000 in software costs, according to the request. Following the death of Corey Ruiz, who was fatally shot by a Madison police officer this summer, the community and some city leaders have amplified their call to implement body-worn cameras. City leaders have oscillated in recent years on implementing them, citing costs, records management, police union conditions and effective policy. City Council President Sabrina Madison introduced a new workgroup this week, the latest of many city committees formed to make recommendations on police use of force and body-worn cameras. The Office of the Independent Monitor, which investigates police misconduct, requested nearly double the cost to continue — mostly to fund its data analyst position, and for additional case management staff and software. Madison's Finance Committee members rejected money for a data analyst and for police oversight members to attend a national conference. In the Mayor’s Office, Rhodes-Conway anticipates cutting $37,000 for the air quality monitoring program, which would mainly affect how the collected data is displayed for residents. City Council members are also facing cuts to their annual salaries of $1,330 each. They are currently paid $17,000 a year. In the Department of Civil Rights, around $61,000 in funding is at risk for the Language Access Program, offering assistance to bilingual residents. The cut isn’t a perfect solution, outgoing Director Norman Davis said, especially given that the program and its three staff members have been experiencing high numbers of requests from residents, but it will prevent critical positions and programs from being eliminated, he said. In the City Clerk’s Office, a 2% cut looks like only one election official per polling place next year for the two scheduled elections. Clerk Lydia McComas is hoping to add two municipal clerk positions next year to prepare for the 2028 presidential election and “reduce operational risk during a period of unprecedented workload and scrutiny.” In the Attorney’s Office, staff might no longer be able to attend out-of-state conferences, and funding could be eliminated to fund a University of Wisconsin-Madison Law School prosecution intern and two full-time legal clerks. A 2% cut would also mean the agency couldn’t post for new positions; the entire city would face a hiring freeze to comply with the projected fiscal constraints. In Municipal Court, there could be reduced security, which would significantly adjust hearing schedules. In the Information Technology department, staff could lose access to Zoom. The Employee Assistance Program, which provides therapy services to city employees, could lose $10,000 in training and mediation funding. The city plans to continue supporting the operations of the new men’s shelter on the north side, which will be run by Porchlight Inc. However, funding for organizations contracted to provide crisis intervention, child and youth services, neighborhood support, older adult services and housing stability would decrease. Cuts also reduce funding for childcare tuition assistance to account for fewer families meeting the qualifications for the city program. In the Parks Division, a 2% cut would amount to $377,000, which could result in reduced beach cleanup, drinking fountain and portable toilet access, reduced trash cleanup and fewer seasonal staff at parks and cemeteries. Madison’s Board of Park Commissioners plans to discuss the golf course’s upgrades, which include a new clubhouse, beer garden and stormwater improvements. The Odana Hills Golf Course will be closed for the remainder of the 2027 season for planned reconstruction regardless of budget cuts. Superintendent Eric Knepp suspects the agency will bring in less revenue because of that, so funding for hourly staff will be cut. Knepp predicts the project will provide a “significant opportunity to secure a stronger financial future for the Golf Enterprise Fund,” and rates will be reviewed at some point later this year, likely resulting in slight increases. The city plans to host a ribbon-cutting ceremony later this month to celebrate the opening of the new Imagination Center library at Reindahl Park, but it’s unclear what cuts could look like until after the facility is open, Library Director Tana Elias said. At the city’s other nine library locations scattered throughout Madison, Sunday hours could be eliminated to save $209,000. Elias also recommended reduced access to databases and streaming services and a 75% reduction in programming, amounting to $139,000, but it’s possible private donations could support some efforts. The Streets Division might eliminate its $74,000 partnership with Sustain Dane to pick up food scraps, and could increase fees for recycling and urban forestry. The agency could also downsize seasonal staff — reducing summer hours — and eliminate vacant positions, which could hamper citywide response to severe weather events. Snow removal on shared-use paths could be reduced to during business hours only. Across the city’s Engineering Corps, which includes the landfill and sewer and stormwater utilities, several proposed cuts could mean higher fees and adjustments to infrastructure training programs. To account for a 2% cut, residents could pay $1.60 more per month for sewerage treatment and an additional 39 cents a month for stormwater. Metro Transit General Manager Jamie Acton said an estimated $9.4 million increase in costs to continue current services comes from projected inflation, wages, benefits, fuel, contracted paratransit services, parts and inventory, and software. The Department of Transportation plans to reduce its efforts to secure grant funding and support from consultants, saving about $15,000. Metro Transit General Manager Jamie Acton reported an increase in paratransit ridership, sparking the need for a review of current operations ahead of a new contract bid for the service next July. The agency’s projected $93 million budget — comprising bus rapid transit, paratransit and fixed routes — is subsidized by the city, and the department could save around $4.2 million. Acton anticipates a $3 million increase in revenue next year from a federal tax refund for the electric buses. But service will likely be reduced along fixed and bus rapid transit routes with low ridership during early mornings and late nights, as will holiday hours on weekdays. Changes could take place as early as this winter, Acton said, warning city leadership that it’s likely annual operations could exceed $100 million by 2028.

title: Madison Metro Transit cuts could affect early bird, night owl riders - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Reductions in early morning, late night and holiday service for Metro Transit riders are set to begin this winter as city agencies attempt to lower their projected spending ahead of next year. The service cuts, approved unanimously by the city’s Transportation Commission last month , are designed to curb the amount of overtime Metro staff are working, especially in the early morning, when some staff must be on-site 45 minutes before the first bus pulls out of the agency’s garage on Ingersoll Street. The cuts are set to take effect in December following last month’s vote. In October, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway will introduce her 2027 budget plans for all city agencies, which must be approved by the City Council. Regular service along Route C, which runs from the University of Wisconsin-Madison to the city’s far east side, would start in December around 5 a.m. on weekdays and 6 a.m. on weekends. Service along Route D from the Dane County Regional Airport to Verona, would begin just before 6 a.m. on weekends. Weekend start times on Route G, which runs along Stoughton Road, and Route H, which connects south and west Madison, would be pushed back by 30 minutes or fewer. “Service will continue to be structured to ensure most transit customers can reach workplaces downtown and nearby before 6 a.m. on weekdays, and 7 a.m. on weekends,” a Metro planning staff report says. “Some trips may be shortened instead of eliminated entirely to better balance operational savings with customer demand.” Proposed reductions in weekend operations on the J, L and O lines would be the steepest of all cuts in terms of total operating time, with anticipated drops between 13% and 20% because of later start times and earlier end times. Route L, which serves the city’s new shelter for unhoused men on Bartillon Drive, would still start service before the shelter’s daytime closing window, and evening trips on the line would continue until the close of intake, the memo says. Routes P and S would also see shorter weekend service. The cuts would not affect the city’s current bus rapid transit line, Route A, or its planned future bus rapid transit line, Route B. Holiday service would be lower on most federal holidays, as well as Ho-Chunk Day (the day after Thanksgiving). The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. The service changes were based largely on existing ridership levels rather than geographic areas, Metro interim planning manager Connor Mountford told the Transportation Commission. “It was really just the time and the ability to generate savings with the least impact on our ridership,” Mountford said. Metro estimates the cuts would affect an average of 13 riders on weekdays, as well as around 100 riders on Saturdays and 60 on Sundays. Cuts to Route C boardings in the early morning, for instance, would affect around four riders on weekends, but around seven on Saturdays and three or four on Sundays, with a similar pattern for Route D. Agency leaders opted for reductions on the J, L and O lines over further cuts to service on the G and H lines due to “concerns over equity impacts,” Mountford added. Citing inflation and rising fuel costs, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway directed city agencies this summer to propose 2% service reductions next year to help balance the budget rather than ask voters to approve another referendum , as city leaders did in 2024. Elected officials on the Transportation Commission lamented the need for cuts, blaming state spending limits like the “Expenditure Restraint Incentive Program,” which provides monetary benefits to local governments that hold spending increases under a certain threshold. “This is not what we want to do. This is what we have to do,” west side Ald. Barbara Harrington-McKinney said at last month’s meeting. “This is not what the departments want to do. It's what they have to do.” Metro’s approved day-to-day operating budget increased from $78.2 million last year to $84.6 million this year, and the agency is proposing a $92 million budget next year, which includes the 2% service cut. The proposed $9.4 million increase is driven by growth in wages and benefits, rising fuel and power costs, “general inflation of contracted paratransit services,” parts and inventory, software and hardware licensing, and operating supplies, according to the agency’s budget document. Metro Transit's 2% service cuts come in response to Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway's directive that agencies reduce anticipated spending amid a potential budget crunch. Metro’s proposed service cuts, along with changes to facilities leasing and using federal grant dollars for vehicle maintenance supplies and tools, are expected to save an anticipated $2 million next year. title: Madison’s next mayor: Who's announced so far? - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Former Dane County Board member April Kigeya announced her bid to be Madison’s mayor this week, joining a growing list of candidates hoping to replace Satya Rhodes-Conway next spring. Rhodes-Conway, first elected in 2019, announced this summer that she’s seeking a third four-year term. Several other community leaders and former local government officials have entered the race since her announcement, including former City Council members Brian Benford and Syed Abbas. Rhodes-Conway is running her re-election campaign on her work building housing in Madison, expanding bus rapid transit, and pushing for safer speeds and traffic infrastructure. The mayor formerly sat on the City Council from 2007 to 2013 representing parts of the north side and participated in sustainability and food access committees before seeking the mayor’s office. Brian Benford stepped back after two terms on the Madison City Council but said he felt called to action after the death of Corey Ruiz. Benford, also a former north side representative, spoke with the Cap Times about why he’s getting back into local politics after stepping back in 2023 to make space for younger leaders. In an interview, he said the lack of leadership following the Madison police shooting of Corey Ruiz on July 22 has inspired him to throw his hat into the ring and run a campaign fueled by the “people’s power.” Benford has decades of experience as a social worker and, more recently, as a success coach for UW-Madison’s Odyssey Project. He described himself as a nontraditional politician and is running his campaign on social justice, racial equity and transparency. Abbas, a former City Council president, announced his candidacy in late August. Abbas works as the deputy legislative director for the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. His platform priorities include housing, fiscal responsibility, social and environmental justice, and transportation. The former City Council president said he wants to increase pathways to own homes and condos, reduce property taxes and expand regional transit. Kigeya is running her platform on challenging Madison’s reputation as a city with affordable housing, good paying jobs and a responsive city government. As mayor, she said, she hopes to prioritize reforming city government so it “listens, responds and delivers for working people.” “The challenges facing our city are real. But so is our ability to solve them,” she said in a press release. “When we listen to one another, bring people together, and put working families at the center of our decisions, we can build One Madison, where all of us belong and all of us can thrive.” One City Schools CEO and Founder Kaleem Caire is also running for mayor. Caire said he plans to officially announce his campaign soon but told the Cap Times he’s been thinking about running since the 1990s. Voters will cast ballots next spring for a leader responsible for a local government corps of about 3,000 workers who serve about 300,000 people. Mayoral terms are four years and there’s no term limits for the position. The mayor’s role is essentially to act as the city’s chief executive officer, responsible for recommending policy to the City Council, breaking tie votes and vetoing legislation. The mayor also fulfills an executive role by ensuring municipal laws are enforced and that city officers and employees do their jobs. The mayor also appoints the city’s department leaders and some committee members, and chooses deputy mayors who act as liaisons for the agencies. Community members have been increasingly critical of Rhodes-Conway lately, especially in the wake of Ruiz’s death and the city’s response to the memorial encampment that was set up this summer to remember Ruiz and protest police violence. Some have called on the mayor and other elected leaders to resign after city officials reopened Williamson and South Baldwin streets early last month, and after City Council members rejected additional funding for police oversight. Rhodes-Conway was first elected in 2019 and said what’s happening in the federal government is partially why she wants to run for another term. Half of the council will be up for election again in April — the odd-numbered districts — in addition to the mayor. A primary election will be held in February, and the two candidates with the most votes in each race will advance to the April general election. Aside from police accountability and racial disparities in Madison, voters will likely weigh several other persistent issues in the spring election. Among them are affordable housing, public safety, community input, transparency, municipal spending and social justice.

title: April Kigeya launches mayoral campaign focused on community voices - Madison365
text: Former Dane County Board Supervisor April Kigeya officially launched her campaign for mayor of Madison as she strives to make a city for all residents. On Sept. 10, Kigeya announced her campaign for mayor and held a launch event at Hayes Place, 1145 N. Sherman Ave. She is among the candidates challenging incumbent Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway, who is seeking a third term. Other candidates include former Alders Syed Abbas and Brian Benford, as well as One City Schools founder Kaleem Caire. Kigeya used the campaign launch as a community mixer, giving attendees an opportunity to get to know one another. She described herself as a “relationship builder” who works to bring people together. “I didn’t want a traditional press conference … I wanted this to be a space where you could meet people that you wouldn’t have otherwise met,” Kigeya said. “I mean, you’re probably standing next to someone right now that you probably don’t even know.” Her approach to the campaign launch is emblematic of her priorities for her potential mayoralship. On her campaign website, Kigeya lists seven priorities, with the very first being a community-led government. The first tenet of her priorities — community-led government — states that the “people closest to a problem should have a meaningful role in solving it.” Kigeya aims to have a more transparent process in decisions that involves community input. “I’ve seen what Madison can do, and I’ve also seen the work that we still have to do,” Kigeya said. “I also believe that the people most impacted by the problems are the ones who can come up with the solutions.” Kigeya’s intended process for a more community-led government involves neighborhood advisory councils with meaningful influence, participatory budgeting that gives residents a direct voice, a regular listening session with the mayor and public action reports to show what happened after engagement, her campaign site states. Her second priority is “Safe Communities,” which includes fully staffing police, fire and EMS departments; strengthening crisis response and mental health co-response; investing in violence prevention and youth mentorship; and building neighborhood partnerships. Her third priority is increasing investment, training and partnerships for mental health services and response. Fourth is attainable housing, which Kigeya stressed is not the same as “affordable housing.” “Affordability, that’s a label,” Kigeya said. “What’s affordable to me may not be affordable to you. I feel like we need to look at attainable housing across all income levels, across all seniors, because there are people that are in their house right now that may not be able to stay in their house, whether it’s based on property taxes going up, whether it’s based on their next paycheck might look different, and that’s going to change.” Kigeya took a jab at the metric of affordable housing in Madison. The city measures success in affordable housing based on how many are built, then pats itself on its back without much reflection on whether it meets the overall needs of residents, Kigeya said. While she does not have an alternative measure right now, Kigeya is set on finding a new metric. Her campaign site lists that the city should work towards growing the housing supply across all income levels, create practical pathways to homeownership, help longtime residents remain in their neighborhoods and pair development with clear measures of affordability and access. Her fifth priority is improving transportation, sixth is providing opportunities for residents regardless of the zip code of the neighborhood and, finally, a government residents can trust. Kigeya said her policies will be based on lived experiences. She cited her own struggles as a single mother of four kids worrying about stability. “I think we rely too much on, and not that it’s not that it’s not important, but we rely too much on just the person’s credentials and not taking lived experience into consideration and not looking at the people who actually live in the city, whether their voice matters.,” Kigeya said. “I feel like people in the city, their voice matters, and I want to bring that and incorporate that into the campaign.” The primary election for the mayoral race will be held in February 2027, where the two candidates with the most votes will advance to the April general election.

title: Disabled Madison woman displaced from home with limited accessible options
text: MADISON, Wis. -- Julie Blasky loved her unit in the Park Cedar Apartments. "I was thriving, I was building a home," Blasky said. She had been living in the ADA compliant and wheelchair accessible space for three years when this August, she started feeling a vibration. Blasky told the property's management, who came to her apartment to see the issue for themselves. "They were able to observe vibration on the countertops, on the walls, and on the floors," Blasky said. That vibration has been harming Blasky's health. "I have a disability that causes spastic or tight, restricted muscles," Blasky said. "That vibration through the floor is coming right up through my wheelchair, right into my body... I've been to urgent care, I've developed like a cough or like a weakness in my lungs, sort of from the constriction." The vibration comes from recently-installed equipment adjacent to Blasky's home. Specifically, Blasky cited the refrigerators being used by a soon-to-be-open grocery store, Maurer's Urban Market. Maurer's reached an agreement back in 2023 to open a store at the location with the City of Madison. That March, the Common Council approved the city's purchase of the space and lease to Maurer's. The city remains Maurer's landlord. In announcing the agreement, Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway called it a major step forward in securing access to healthy food in South Madison for decades to come. At the time, the Pick 'N Save right across the street was said to be closing at the end of the year. However, that grocer remains up and running. News 3 Now reached out to the City of Madison and was told the city was not directly involved in Blasky's situation. City Communications Manager Dylan Brogan said the grocer is in charge, and pointed to Movin' Out, the nonprofit housing developer that lists Park Cedar as a featured project on its website . Movin' Out has been assisting Blasky in recent weeks after the vibration started. But so far, none of the alternatives offered have been able to fully meet her needs. "Unfortunately, there probably isn't an easy fix," Blasky said. Blasky said there is a difference between ADA compliant apartments and "accessible" apartments. She stressed that what might be deemed as accessible by one person or group of people doesn't necessarily mean it's accessible for someone like her, who is wheelchair-bound. In a statement to News 3 now, Movin' Out said it was deeply concerned about the unexpected negative impact on Blasky resulting from the adjacent grocery installation and operation. "Ideally we would be able to place Julie in another unit with accessibility features that are equivalent to those she currently has," said CEO Kathryne Auerback. "We are in communication with WHEDA to understand other options or alternatives. In the meantime, we are providing short-term housing for Julie." That short term housing is not ADA-compliant. Amid the uncertainty of when she'll have a new long-term home that meets her needs, Blasky said she still has to pay rent at the apartment she is displaced from. "That home meant so much more to me and is really a diamond in the rough, and now I don't have anything," Blasky said. News 3 Now reached out to Wisconsin Management Company, the manager of Park Cedar, for comment but did not hear anything back. title: Homeowners push back on Milwaukee Street project assessments
text: Sewer, road costs homeowners thousands MADISON (WKOW) -- The City of Madison plans to reconstruct Milwaukee Street and replace aging sewer and water pipes, but some homeowners are facing special assessments of more than $7,000. Many homeowners are questioning why developers of a housing project across the street aren't paying more of the cost. Neighbor Troy Stehr raised that concern during last Wednesday's Public Works meeting. "It's really hard for me to accept that the sanitary and water changes we're experiencing are not the result of like over 1,000 additional units being developed on that property," Stehr said. The city says developers are paying their share and the roadwork is needed to replace sewer and water pipes dating back to the 1950s. "I think it's the long-term prudent thing to do, but I definitely am concerned for the people on the street that are having to absorb that big amount," District 15 Alder Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford said. The city says special assessments are nothing new. The practice dates back decades and is common among cities. Officials say final assessments are typically lower than preliminary estimates unless homeowners request additional work. Special assessments typically account for 6% to 8% of the cost of a full reconstruction project, with the city covering the rest. For individual homeowners, however, that can still mean thousands of dollars. For Milwaukee Street, homeowners can pay their assessment in one lump sum by the end of October 2028 or choose a 15-year payment plan at 4.5% interest.

Goals of Kigeya’s candidacy include violence prevention, expanding mobile crisis responses and holding open office hours.  Rhodes-Conway Rhodes-Conway has been in office since 2019 and is promoting her work on affordable housing and modern transit system in her re-election campaign. Rhodes-Conway blamed COVID-19 for delaying priorities in her first term and the focus on housing affordability in her second term for neglecting other areas, according to the Wisconsin State Journal. Brian Benford Brian Benford, former City Council member and alderman, stepped back from Madison politics three years ago, but in August he told the Cap Times he had to run for mayor after a “lack of city leadership” in the wake of the Corey Ruiz shooting .  If elected, Benford said he will focus on supporting minority and marginalized groups in Madison, only running for one term in order to pass leadership to the younger generation. Syed Abbas Syed Abbas, former Common Council president and alderman, currently serves as Wisconsin’s Deputy Legislative Director at the Department of Health Services.  “We need to make housing more affordable, strengthen our neighborhoods, support economic opportunity, invest wisely in public safety and infrastructure, and make sure every Madisonian has a chance to succeed,” Abbas said on his campaign website.  He notes the end goal of his mayoral run is making Madison a place people settle in by lowering property taxes, making homeownership more achievable and decreasing homelessness through city-run supportive housing programs. Jonny Hinds Johnny Hinds, known as Jon Hinds, founded the Monkey Bar Gym in Madison and has been outspoken on Facebook about police brutality, the spending of city funds and homelessness. “Because ultimately, I think we all want the same things: we don't want people being shot on our streets,” Hinds wrote on a post . “We don't want families feeling ignored or forgotten. We don't want police officers put in situations where they have to make a split-second decision they'll live with forever.” Larry Williams Larry “Ace” Williams is a food service and hospitality director who submitted his paperwork close to Kigeya and Hinds. Not much else is known about him, according to 77 Square Miles .  The spring primary election will be held Feb. 16, 2027 and the spring election will be April 6, 2027, with all candidate options being finalized on Jan. 5, 2027.

title: Clarion Partners, Vermilion Development and Quartz Lake Capital Celebrate the Grand Opening of The - MultifamilyBiz
text: MADISON, WI - Clarion Partners, a leading real estate investment manager and partially owned subsidiary of Franklin Templeton, Vermilion Development, a full-service real estate investment and development company, and Quartz Lake Capital, a private equity real estate investor and manager, recently hosted an official ribbon-cutting event with the residents, elected officials, distinguished guests, and project team at the newly opened multifamily community The Duncan, located within a federally-designated Qualified Opportunity Zone at 1625 Lock Lane in Madison, Wisconsin. Located on approximately 8.2 acres along Madison’s Isthmus, the 309-unit property offers residents a distinctive lakeside living experience with proximity to downtown Madison. Designed to reflect the lifestyle and unique character of the city, The Duncan offers two fitness centers, bicycle storage, a pet spa and dog run, purpose-built coworking and breakout spaces, a community garden, heated parking and two rooftop terraces featuring grills, firepits and views of Lake Mendota. Residents also have immediate access to Tenney Park, a 37-acre waterfront park offering recreational amenities including tennis, pickleball and basketball courts, a boat launch, playgrounds and an ice-skating rink. For Marwa Shaaban, a new resident of The Duncan, the waterfront setting and sense of community have already made the property feel like home. “The location has been incredible. Tenney Park is within walking distance, and Lake Mendota is right in our backyard,” said Shaaban. “When my sister visited this summer, we walked out to watch the sunset and she said, ‘I didn’t know you had heaven in your backyard.’ That really captures what it feels like living here. The staff have also been fantastic — they are communicative, accessible and have really helped create a sense of community.” Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway also marked the milestone by proclaiming August 13, 2026, “The Duncan Day” in the City of Madison, recognizing the new waterfront community and the partners who helped bring it to life. The Duncan adds 309 new homes to Madison at a time when the city continues to experience significant demand for housing. Madison projects the addition of more than 9,300 households — approximately 18,400 people — by 2030 and has established a goal of creating 15,000 new homes by then. “We believe residents will enjoy the many amenities that The Duncan provides, from its thoughtful design and social spaces to its sweeping views of Lake Mendota and Tenney Park,” said Clarion Partners Senior Vice President Ian McKay. “We’re proud to partner with Vermilion and Quartz Lake to bring this beautiful new property to life.” “Two years ago, this was a vision on paper and a construction site. Today, it is 309 homes,” said Dave Cocagne, President and CEO of Vermilion Development. “But housing is about much more than a unit count. Our mission at Vermilion is to create spaces that enrich people’s lives, and The Duncan was designed specifically for Madison — connected to the lake, Tenney Park, trails, bikes and downtown. The most rewarding part begins now, as residents make these spaces their homes and build their lives here.” “The Duncan is a standout addition to Madison’s growing residential market, combining modern amenities with an unparalleled lakeside setting,” remarked Alison Gorham, Vice President & Director of Wisconsin Operations at McShane Construction. “As our first project with Vermilion, we are proud to celebrate the strong partnership that brought this project from concept to completion.” The site also has a unique connection to Madison history. On May 14, 1950, President Harry Truman visited the property to dedicate Filene House, then headquarters of the Credit Union National Association. During his remarks, Truman spoke about cooperation to help address the nation’s housing needs. More than seven decades later, The Duncan similarly reflects the work of numerous public- and private-sector partners. The development brought together Vermilion Development, Clarion Partners and Quartz Lake Capital as equity partners, CIBC as lender, Potter Lawson as architect, and McShane Construction Company as general contractor. JLL sourced the project’s equity and debt, and Greystar as property manager. The Duncan includes studio, one-, two- and three-bedroom residences, including townhome options. Many residences feature views of the Wisconsin State Capitol, Tenney Park, or Lake Mendota. Sustainability and energy efficiency are also incorporated into the project’s design. The community includes ENERGY STAR appliances, occupancy sensors in applicable common areas, efficient natural-gas water heating and WaterSense plumbing fixtures. “The Duncan is the result of an extraordinary amount of collaboration and persistence,” Cocagne added. “From the City of Madison to our investment, lending, design and construction partners, many people shared the vision for what this property could become. We are grateful to everyone who helped take The Duncan from an idea to a drawing to a construction site — and now, most importantly, to a place people call home.”

title: Madison police commission weighs bid to fire officer who shot Ruiz - The Cap Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. In a complaint filed with the city’s Police and Fire Commission, members of a local political action committee are calling for the firing of Madison Police Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson, who fatally shot Corey Ruiz in July at the intersection of Williamson and South Baldwin streets. Blacks for Political and Social Action of Dane County filed the complaint shortly after the July 22 shooting. The commission is the city’s only entity under state law with the authority to fire a police officer. Baitinger-Peterson shot Ruiz, a 38-year-old Black man, after officers were dispatched to the Marquette neighborhood for a report of someone checking parked cars, according to police. The complaint alleges Baitinger-Peterson violated Police Department policies, including use of force and de-escalation, and calls on the commission to also issue “severe” disciplinary suspensions or terminations for three other officers who were involved in the incident over failing to prevent the “unnecessary deadly force.” Mary Schauf, the commission’s president, said in a meeting Tuesday she’s launched a preliminary investigation into whether the commission has legal authority to adjudicate the complaint and whether Blacks for Political and Social Action of Dane County has a legal right to file the complaint. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Kate Harrell, an attorney with the Wisconsin Professional Police Association, is representing Baitinger-Peterson. The Rev. David Hart, an attorney and president of Blacks for Political and Social Action of Dane County, and Kirbie Mack, the group’s vice president, are representing the organization in its complaint against Baitinger-Peterson. The commission currently has four members appointed by the mayor and approved by the City Council. A fifth seat is vacant. One of the commission’s four members, Azure Fudge Hart, has recused herself from weighing in on the group’s complaint; she is married to Hart. Harrell argued in a brief filed with the commission this week that the organization doesn’t have legal standing to be a complainant and requested the complaint be dismissed. In response to Schauf’s preliminary investigation, Hart and Mack argued in a brief that they do meet the legal requirements to file a complaint, citing their interests in the safety of their families, their communities and themselves. “How could concern for the killing of a citizen by a police officer not be sufficient?” Hart and Mack wrote. Tuesday’s hearing lasted about 10 minutes and focused on scheduling a time for both sides to file additional information in November and continue the hearing in December. Attorney Ben Crump leads a chant of "Justice for Corey" as he stands besides family members of Corey Ruiz during Ruiz's funeral at Fountain of Life Covenant Church in Madison. Ruiz was fatally shot by Madison Police Officer Kiel Baitinger-Peterson on July 22. About 30 people submitted written public comment to the commission ahead of the hearing. All but one community member wrote in support of the complaint, with some demanding Baitinger-Peterson’s removal from the police force. Harrell, the attorney representing Baitinger-Peterson, asked the commission in her brief to delay the complaint proceedings until any potential criminal proceedings against Baitinger-Peterson are resolved. The state Department of Justice’s Division of Criminal Investigation is reviewing Baitinger-Peterson's shooting of Ruiz under a state law that requires an outside agency to investigate officer-involved deaths. Once the investigation is completed, the case file will go to Dane County District Attorney Ismael Ozanne, who will decide whether to charge Baitinger-Peterson with a crime. The Department of Justice’s investigation is separate from any internal affairs review by the Madison Police Department or the complaint process through the city’s Police and Fire Commission. Ruiz’s death renewed national attention on police violence and sparked protests throughout the city. An encampment was established at the intersection on Willy Street where Ruiz was shot, increasing tensions between police, advocates and city leaders. Baitinger-Peterson has almost 11 years of law enforcement experience. Madison Police Chief John Patterson has described him as a veteran officer. Madison Police Chief John Patterson in April called funding city-wide use of body-worn cameras his No. 1 request for the department. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway included about $415,000 in her September capital budget plan to purchase 220 cameras, supporting equipment and training. Baitinger-Peterson came up through the Police Department's internship program, according to the department's 2020 annual report. The department hired him in 2015, and he served as a patrol officer until 2022, Patterson previously said. Baitinger-Peterson spent a year as a neighborhood police officer for the Darbo-Worthington neighborhood on the east side. Starting in 2023 and until February, Baitinger-Peterson was a member of the Police Department's gang and neighborhood crime abatement team. Then Baitinger-Peterson became part of the Central District Community Police Team this past winter, serving the downtown area. Most of Madison’s police officers don’t use body-worn cameras, and the current public footage of the shooting comes from bystander video posted to social media. Patterson in April called funding city-wide use of body-worn cameras his No. 1 request for the department. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway included about $415,000 in her September capital budget plan to purchase 220 cameras, supporting equipment and training. The proposal outlines a three-year deployment, starting with equipping officers in the North District next year. Ruiz’s family has called for state lawmakers to pass a body-worn camera mandate for police officers. State Rep. Shelia Stubbs, D-Madison, previously said she’s working with Ruiz’s family and their attorneys, including nationally renowned civil rights lawyer Ben Crump, on drafting legislation that could be introduced next session.
